topics.title: Letters, stress and written accents
topics.summary: Read Spanish spelling, locate stress and use common written accents.
topics.guidance: Treat spelling and sound separately. This written chapter introduces pronunciation patterns; it does not assess listening or accent.
learningGoals: Recognise ñ, silent h and common letter combinations.
Apply ordinary stress and accent rules.
Distinguish common words using a diacritical accent.

rules.title: Read letters and combinations
rules.explanation: H is normally silent in Spanish words. Ñ represents a different sound from n. Qu before e/i normally has a silent u; gü before e/i marks a pronounced u.
rules.pattern: h; n / ñ; que / qui; güe / güi
examples: El niño lee. — The boy reads.
El pingüino nada. — The penguin swims.
commonMistakes: Do not remove ñ or the diaeresis from a word that needs it.

rules.title: Find ordinary word stress
rules.explanation: Without an accent mark, most words ending in a vowel, n or s have penultimate stress; other ordinary consonant endings usually have final stress. Consonant clusters and some borrowed words need separate attention.
rules.pattern: ca-sa; ha-blan; pa-pel
examples: La casa tiene un patio. — The house has a courtyard.
El papel es azul. — The paper is blue.
commonMistakes: Written accents can override the default pattern.

rules.title: Write an accent when required
rules.explanation: Final-stressed words ending in a vowel, n or s normally need a written accent; penultimate-stressed words with other ordinary consonant endings need one. Antepenultimate stress always takes an accent. A stressed i/u beside an unstressed open vowel also takes one.
rules.pattern: café; árbol; teléfono; río
examples: Bebo café. — I drink coffee.
El río está cerca. — The river is nearby.
commonMistakes: Capital letters retain required accents.

rules.title: Distinguish short words
rules.explanation: A diacritical accent distinguishes certain stressed words: tú/tu, él/el, mí/mi, sí/si, té/te and sé/se. Direct and indirect interrogative words also carry accents.
rules.pattern: tú = you; tu = your; qué = what
examples: Tú tienes tu llave. — You have your key.
No sé qué quiere. — I do not know what he or she wants.
commonMistakes: Ordinary monosyllables such as fue do not take an accent.

introduction: Spanish has five vowel letters and a separate letter ñ. The digraphs ch and ll are combinations of letters, not separate alphabet letters.
Pronunciation varies legitimately: seseo, distinción and different pronunciations of ll/y are not errors. Written stress rules still apply across those varieties.

topics.title: Noun gender and plurals
topics.summary: Learn nouns with their gender and form common singular and plural noun phrases.
topics.guidance: Learn the article with a new noun. Endings help but do not determine every noun’s gender.
learningGoals: Use masculine and feminine noun phrases.
Form common plurals in -s and -es.
Keep determiners and adjectives in agreement.

rules.title: Learn noun gender
rules.explanation: Learn el libro and la mesa as whole phrases. Some frequent exceptions include el día, el problema and la mano. Many -ción and -dad nouns are feminine.
rules.pattern: el día; la mano; la ciudad
examples: El problema es difícil. — The problem is difficult.
La mano está limpia. — The hand is clean.
commonMistakes: An -a ending does not automatically make a noun feminine.

rules.title: Add -s after common vowel endings
rules.explanation: Nouns ending in an unstressed vowel or stressed e normally add -s. Stressed a/o also normally add -s. Other endings can have special patterns.
rules.pattern: casa → casas; café → cafés
examples: Hay dos casas. — There are two houses.
Pedimos tres cafés. — We order three coffees.
commonMistakes: Do not add -ses to café or sofá.

rules.title: Form common consonant plurals
rules.explanation: Many common nouns ending in a consonant add -es. Final z becomes c before -es. Written accents can change to preserve the original stress pattern.
rules.pattern: papel → papeles; luz → luces; canción → canciones
examples: Necesito lápices. — I need pencils.
Las canciones son nuevas. — The songs are new.
commonMistakes: Do not write luzes or retain a needless accent in canciones.

rules.title: Agree throughout a noun phrase
rules.explanation: Articles and variable adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number. Some nouns such as estudiante use the same form for a man or a woman; the article marks the intended reference.
rules.pattern: la estudiante; los libros nuevos
examples: Las ventanas están abiertas. — The windows are open.
El estudiante está preparado. — The male student is ready.
commonMistakes: Plural agreement extends beyond the noun itself.

introduction: Grammatical gender belongs to a noun; it does not describe the physical sex of objects. Many -o nouns are masculine and many -a nouns feminine, with important exceptions.
Plural endings depend on spelling and stress. Learn exceptional and variable patterns from a dictionary rather than applying one rule to every borrowed word.

topics.title: Articles and al / del
topics.summary: Choose definite and indefinite articles and contract a/de with el.
topics.guidance: Use the intended meaning as well as gender and number. An article can be grammatically possible but wrong for the stated meaning.
learningGoals: Choose definite and indefinite noun phrases.
Use al and del correctly.
Recognise stressed-a nouns and common article omissions.

rules.title: Identify the intended referent
rules.explanation: Use el/la/los/las according to gender and number when the intended meaning is the specified noun.
rules.pattern: el libro; la puerta; los zapatos; las llaves
examples: Cierra la puerta. — Close the door.
Los zapatos están mojados. — The shoes are wet.
commonMistakes: Do not choose an indefinite article when translating an explicitly definite phrase.

rules.title: Introduce a noun
rules.explanation: Un and una mean a/an; unos and unas can mean some. Choose according to the noun, not English spelling.
rules.pattern: un coche; una idea; unos vasos; unas mesas
examples: Necesito una idea. — I need an idea.
Hay unos vasos aquí. — There are some glasses here.
commonMistakes: Un is not the article for an ordinary feminine noun.

rules.title: Join a/de with the article el
rules.explanation: Write al for a + el and del for de + el. Do not contract a él or de él, where él is a pronoun. Proper titles that retain El can require separate spelling.
rules.pattern: al mercado; del vecino; a él
examples: Voy al mercado. — I am going to the market.
Este libro es de él. — This book is his.
commonMistakes: Al and del already contain the article; do not add another el.

rules.title: Notice article use in context
rules.explanation: Immediately before a feminine noun starting with stressed a/ha, definite el is usual: el agua fría. The plural returns to las. A bare profession normally follows ser unless modified or evaluated.
rules.pattern: el agua fría; las aguas; es médica
examples: El aula está vacía. — The classroom is empty.
Mi tía es médica. — My aunt is a doctor.
commonMistakes: El agua remains feminine; write fría, not frío.

introduction: Definite el/la/los/las usually point to an identifiable referent or a class. Indefinite un/una/unos/unas introduce or classify less specific referents.
Only the article el contracts with a/de. The pronoun él remains separate. Stressed-a feminine nouns retain feminine agreement even when immediately preceded by el.

topics.title: Subject pronouns and ser
topics.summary: Introduce people and use present-tense ser with matching subjects.
topics.guidance: The exercises specify person and number. Tú, vos and usted vary by region and relationship; no variety is treated as inferior.
learningGoals: Identify subject pronouns.
Conjugate present-tense ser.
Use ser for identity, origin, profession and time.

rules.title: Match pronouns to people
rules.explanation: Yo means I; tú is familiar singular you; él/ella mean he/she. Nosotros/nosotras mean we. Ellos/ellas mean they. Use usted/ustedes according to the stated address.
rules.pattern: yo; tú; él/ella; nosotros/as; ellos/as
examples: Yo soy estudiante. — I am a student.
Ella es mi vecina. — She is my neighbour.
commonMistakes: Do not confuse a pronoun’s listener meaning with the verb form it takes.

rules.title: Conjugate singular ser
rules.explanation: Present ser has irregular singular forms: yo soy, tú eres, él/ella/usted es.
rules.pattern: soy; eres; es
examples: Soy de Chile. — I am from Chile.
Usted es la directora. — You are the director.
commonMistakes: Usted takes es, not eres.

rules.title: Conjugate plural ser
rules.explanation: Use nosotros/as somos, vosotros/as sois and ellos/ellas/ustedes son. These forms also work with equivalent noun subjects.
rules.pattern: somos; sois; son
examples: Nosotras somos amigas. — We are friends.
Ustedes son los primeros. — You are the first to arrive.
commonMistakes: Ustedes always takes third-person plural in this course.

rules.title: Classify and identify
rules.explanation: Ser expresses identity, origin, profession and time. Its use is broader than a simple permanent/temporary contrast.
rules.pattern: ser + noun; ser de + origin; es la una / son las dos
examples: Elena es arquitecta. — Elena is an architect.
Son las cuatro. — It is four o’clock.
commonMistakes: Do not use estar merely because a profession or time can change.

introduction: Spanish often omits a subject pronoun when the verb and context identify it. Pronouns remain useful for contrast or clarity.

Usted refers to one listener but uses third-person singular verbs; ustedes refers to several listeners and uses third-person plural. Vosotros/vosotras is familiar plural in much of Spain. Voseo has its own legitimate regional forms.

topics.title: Ser, estar and hay
topics.summary: Distinguish identity, states, locations and existence.
topics.guidance: Ask whether you are identifying something, locating an identified thing, describing a state or introducing what exists.
learningGoals: Conjugate present estar.
Use hay for existence.
Use ser for classification and event location.
Describe states and locate people or objects.

rules.title: Learn present estar
rules.explanation: Use estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis and están. Written accents distinguish several forms.
rules.pattern: yo estoy; tú estás; ella está; nosotros estamos
examples: Estoy en casa. — I am at home.
Ellos están cansados. — They are tired.
commonMistakes: Do not omit the accents in está, estás, estáis or están.

rules.title: Introduce what exists
rules.explanation: Hay means there is/there are. It is impersonal and unchanged before one or several things, typically with indefinite nouns or quantities.
rules.pattern: hay + un/una / plural / quantity
examples: Hay una farmacia. — There is a pharmacy.
Hay tres bancos. — There are three banks.
commonMistakes: Do not make present hay plural to agree with the following noun.

rules.title: Identify or classify
rules.explanation: Ser identifies people/things and expresses origin, material and time. Event locations also normally use ser.
rules.pattern: ser + identity; event + ser en
examples: La reunión es en el salón. — The meeting is in the hall.
Mi mochila es roja. — My backpack is red.
commonMistakes: An event’s location differs from the physical location of an object.

rules.title: Locate and describe states
rules.explanation: Estar locates identified people and objects and expresses many conditions or results. Some adjectives change meaning with ser/estar; context decides.
rules.pattern: estar en + location; estar + state
examples: Las llaves están en el cajón. — The keys are in the drawer.
La sopa está fría. — The soup is cold.
commonMistakes: Do not apply a permanent/temporary slogan to every sentence.

introduction: Ser and estar express different perspectives; permanent versus temporary is an incomplete shortcut. A city’s fixed location uses estar, while a scheduled event’s location normally uses ser.
Hay introduces existence and does not change for a plural noun. Estar locates an identified person or object and agrees with its subject.

topics.title: Regular present-tense verbs
topics.summary: Build regular present forms in -ar, -er and -ir and match the subject.
topics.guidance: Remove the infinitive ending before adding the present ending. The questions explicitly ask for present indicative.
learningGoals: Conjugate regular present verbs.
Distinguish -ar, -er and -ir endings.
Recognise the subject in a sentence.

rules.title: Regular -ar verbs
rules.explanation: Remove -ar and add -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an.
rules.pattern: hablar → hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan
examples: Hablo con mi hermana. — I talk to my sister.
Caminamos al trabajo. — We walk to work.
commonMistakes: Do not retain the infinitive ending before the personal ending.

rules.title: Regular -er verbs
rules.explanation: Remove -er and add -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en.
rules.pattern: comer → como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen
examples: Comes temprano. — You eat early.
Leen el periódico. — They read the newspaper.
commonMistakes: Nosotros -er verbs end in -emos, not -amos.

rules.title: Regular -ir verbs
rules.explanation: Remove -ir and add -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en. The nosotros/vosotros endings differ from -er.
rules.pattern: vivir → vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven
examples: Vivimos junto al mar. — We live by the sea.
Abro la ventana. — I open the window.
commonMistakes: Use vivimos rather than vivemos.

rules.title: Find the subject
rules.explanation: A coordinated group including yo uses first-person plural; usted/ustedes use third-person forms. A question or no does not change the agreement.
rules.pattern: mi hermana y yo → nosotros; ustedes → third-person plural
examples: Mi padre y yo cocinamos. — My father and I cook.
¿Usted trabaja aquí? — Do you work here?
commonMistakes: No auxiliary do is added to a Spanish present question.

introduction: The present indicative describes habits, facts and many current situations. Spanish does not need an equivalent of English do to make ordinary questions or negatives.
The subject may be a pronoun, a noun phrase or a coordinated group. The verb ending must agree even when the subject pronoun is omitted.

topics.title: Irregular and stem-changing present verbs
topics.summary: Learn common irregular present forms and predictable stem changes.
topics.guidance: Use the stated subject and tense. Nosotros/vosotros usually retain the unstressed stem in these present stem-changing patterns.
learningGoals: Use common irregular yo forms.
Apply e→ie and o→ue stem changes.
Use ir, tener and other frequent irregular verbs.

rules.title: Common irregular yo forms
rules.explanation: Some verbs have special first-person forms: hago, pongo, salgo, conozco, sé and doy. Other persons may follow a different pattern.
rules.pattern: hacer → hago; saber → sé
examples: Hago la compra. — I do the shopping.
Sé la respuesta. — I know the answer.
commonMistakes: Do not regularise special forms as haco or sabo.

rules.title: Change stressed e to ie
rules.explanation: Pensar, querer, empezar and cerrar change stressed e to ie in yo/tú/él/ellos forms. Nosotros/vosotros keep the stem vowel.
rules.pattern: pienso / pensamos; quiere / queremos
examples: Pienso en el viaje. — I think about the trip.
Cerramos a las seis. — We close at six.
commonMistakes: The stem change does not usually occur in nosotros/vosotros present forms.

rules.title: Change stressed o to ue
rules.explanation: Poder, dormir, volver and encontrar have o→ue in stressed present stems. Nosotros/vosotros normally retain o.
rules.pattern: puedo / podemos; duermen / dormimos
examples: Puedo ayudarte. — I can help you.
Dormimos ocho horas. — We sleep eight hours.
commonMistakes: Do not write puedemos or duermimos.

rules.title: Learn frequent mixed patterns
rules.explanation: Ir uses voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van. Tener combines tengo with tienes/tiene/tienen and tenemos/tenéis. Pedir changes e→i in stressed present stems.
rules.pattern: voy; tienes; pedimos / piden
examples: Voy al trabajo. — I go to work.
Piden agua. — They ask for water.
commonMistakes: Use the pattern belonging to the actual verb and person.

introduction: A stem change affects a stressed vowel in many present forms but normally not nosotros/vosotros. The verb still takes personal endings.
Some verbs combine patterns: tener has tengo for yo and tienes for tú. Learn each pattern with its infinitive rather than treating every irregular form alike.

topics.title: Adjectives, demonstratives and possessives
topics.summary: Build descriptions and indicate distance and ownership with agreeing forms.
topics.guidance: Agreement follows the described or possessed noun. Demonstrative distance is made explicit in each question.
learningGoals: Agree variable adjectives.
Choose near and more distant demonstratives.
Use possessives according to the possessed noun.

rules.title: Agree adjectives
rules.explanation: Variable adjectives agree in gender and number; adjectives ending in -e often change only for plural.
rules.pattern: un coche rojo; casas rojas; personas inteligentes
examples: La mochila es pesada. — The backpack is heavy.
Los trenes son rápidos. — The trains are fast.
commonMistakes: Do not add a feminine -a to an adjective such as inteligente.

rules.title: Point to something near
rules.explanation: Este/esta/estos/estas refer to things near the speaker in the intended context. They agree with the noun.
rules.pattern: este libro; esta mesa; estos vasos; estas llaves
examples: Esta taza es mía. — This cup is mine.
Estos zapatos son nuevos. — These shoes are new.
commonMistakes: The form depends on the noun, not the speaker’s gender.

rules.title: Point farther away
rules.explanation: Ese/esa/esos/esas commonly indicate something nearer the listener or less close to the speaker. Aquel/aquella/aquellos/aquellas indicate the more distant set in an explicit three-way contrast.
rules.pattern: ese coche; aquella montaña
examples: Ese cuaderno junto a ti es azul. — That notebook beside you is blue.
Aquellas casas a lo lejos son antiguas. — Those houses in the distance are old.
commonMistakes: Distance is contextual; do not declare every use of ese for a distant thing wrong.

rules.title: Match the possessed noun
rules.explanation: Mi/tu/su vary for the number of the possessed noun. Nuestro/vuestro vary for both its gender and number. They do not agree with the owner’s gender.
rules.pattern: mi libro / mis libros; nuestra casa / nuestros hijos
examples: Mi hermano vive aquí. — My brother lives here.
Nuestras hijas estudian. — Our daughters study.
commonMistakes: Use su/sus according to the thing owned, not the number of owners.

introduction: Most descriptive adjectives follow the noun in neutral descriptions. Many change -o to -a; adjectives in -e often have one singular form for both genders.
Este/ese/aquel distinguish perspectives on distance, not an exact number of metres. Possessive su can refer to several owners, so specify or clarify the owner when needed.

rules.title: Agree adjectives
rules.explanation: Variable adjectives agree in gender and number; adjectives ending in -e often change only for plural.
rules.pattern: un coche rojo; casas rojas; personas inteligentes

rules.title: Point to something near
rules.explanation: Este/esta/estos/estas refer to things near the speaker in the intended context. They agree with the noun.
rules.pattern: este libro; esta mesa; estos vasos; estas llaves
examples: Esta taza es mía. — This cup is mine.
Estos zapatos son nuevos. — These shoes are new.
commonMistakes: The form depends on the noun, not the speaker’s gender.

rules.title: Point farther away
rules.explanation: Ese/esa/esos/esas commonly indicate something nearer the listener or less close to the speaker. Aquel/aquella/aquellos/aquellas indicate the more distant set in an explicit three-way contrast.
rules.pattern: ese coche; aquella montaña
examples: Ese cuaderno junto a ti es azul. — That notebook beside you is blue.
Aquellas casas a lo lejos son antiguas. — Those houses in the distance are old.
commonMistakes: Distance is contextual; do not declare every use of ese for a distant thing wrong.

rules.title: Match the possessed noun
rules.explanation: Mi/tu/su vary for the number of the possessed noun. Nuestro/vuestro vary for both its gender and number. They do not agree with the owner’s gender.
rules.pattern: mi libro / mis libros; nuestra casa / nuestros hijos
examples: Mi hermano vive aquí. — My brother lives here.
Nuestras hijas estudian. — Our daughters study.
commonMistakes: Use su/sus according to the thing owned, not the number of owners.

topics.title: Questions and negation
topics.summary: Ask for information, agree question words and construct ordinary negatives.
topics.guidance: Use the requested information or meaning. Spanish negative concord is normal grammar, not an English-style double-negative error.
learningGoals: Select interrogative words.
Agree cuánto and quién where required.
Place no before a finite verb.
Use nadie, nada, nunca and tampoco.

rules.title: Ask for the right information
rules.explanation: Dónde asks where, cuándo when, quién who, cómo how and por qué why. Select according to the information wanted, rather than a fixed word order.
rules.pattern: ¿Dónde…? ¿Cuándo…? ¿Por qué…?
examples: ¿Dónde vive tu abuela? — Where does your grandmother live?
¿Por qué cierran hoy? — Why are they closing today?
commonMistakes: Interrogative por qué is two words and carries an accent.

rules.title: Agree quantity questions
rules.explanation: Cuánto/cuánta/cuántos/cuántas agree with the noun they determine. Cuánto used alone for an amount or price is invariable in that use. Quién has plural quiénes.
rules.pattern: ¿Cuántas sillas? ¿Cuánto cuesta?
examples: ¿Cuántos días tienes? — How many days do you have?
¿Quiénes son? — Who are they?
commonMistakes: Do not use masculine cuántos before a feminine plural noun.

rules.title: Place no before the verb
rules.explanation: In an ordinary negative statement, no goes before the finite verb, with unstressed object/reflexive pronouns between no and that verb. Agreement remains unchanged.
rules.pattern: no + verb; no + pronoun + verb
examples: No trabajo hoy. — I do not work today.
No lo entiendo. — I do not understand it.
commonMistakes: Do not copy English do not or put no after the verb for ordinary negation.

rules.title: Use negative concord
rules.explanation: Nadie means nobody, nada nothing, nunca never and tampoco neither/not either. Compare No viene nadie with Nadie viene; both express nobody coming.
rules.pattern: no + verb + nadie/nada/nunca; nadie/nunca + verb
examples: No veo nada. — I see nothing.
Nadie responde. — Nobody answers.
commonMistakes: Negative words after the verb normally combine with preverbal no.

introduction: Direct written questions use both ¿ and ?. Interrogative words have written accents in direct and indirect questions. Ordinary Spanish questions do not add English do.
No normally precedes the finite verb or its preceding clitic pronouns. A negative word after the verb normally needs preverbal no; a negative word before the verb can make no unnecessary.

topics.title: Gustar and reflexive routines
topics.summary: Express likes and describe everyday pronominal routines.
topics.guidance: With ordinary gustar, the thing liked controls the verb; with a reflexive routine, the person acting controls the verb.
learningGoals: Choose gusta or gustan.
Mark the experiencer with an indirect-object pronoun.
Match reflexive pronouns and present verbs.

rules.title: Agree with what is liked
rules.explanation: Use gusta with a singular noun or one infinitive phrase; use gustan with plural nouns. The experiencer does not control this number choice.
rules.pattern: me gusta el cine / nadar; me gustan las películas
examples: Nos gusta caminar. — We like walking.
Le gustan los libros. — He or she likes books.
commonMistakes: Plural experiencers do not automatically require gustan.

rules.title: Mark the experiencer
rules.explanation: Use me, te, le, nos, os or les for the person experiencing the liking. A mí/a ti/a ella can clarify or contrast, normally alongside the unstressed pronoun.
rules.pattern: a mí me; a ti te; a ustedes les
examples: A mí me gusta el jazz. — I like jazz.
A ustedes les gusta viajar. — You like travelling.
commonMistakes: Do not replace the required indirect pronoun with a subject pronoun.

rules.title: Match routine pronouns
rules.explanation: For a pronominal routine use me/te/se/nos/os/se with yo/tú/él/nosotros/vosotros/ellos. Place it before a simple finite present verb.
rules.pattern: me levanto; te duchas; se acuestan
examples: Me ducho por la mañana. — I shower in the morning.
Nos levantamos temprano. — We get up early.
commonMistakes: Usted and ustedes use se, with singular or plural verbs respectively.

rules.title: Conjugate the routine verb
rules.explanation: The reflexive pronoun does not replace the personal verb ending. Acostarse and despertarse have present stem changes; nosotros/vosotros normally keep the original vowel.
rules.pattern: me acuesto / nos acostamos; se despierta
examples: Ella se despierta a las siete. — She wakes at seven.
Nos acostamos tarde. — We go to bed late.
commonMistakes: Do not combine a yo pronoun with a third-person verb ending.

introduction: Me gusta el pan literally presents bread as pleasing to me. The person who likes it is represented by me/te/le/nos/os/les, while el pan is the grammatical subject.
Many routine verbs use reflexive or other pronominal constructions. Learn levantarse, ducharse and acostarse with the pronoun; some other uses of these verbs can be transitive.

topics.title: The preterite: completed past events
topics.summary: Form regular and common irregular preterites to present past events as completed wholes.
topics.guidance: Each form task requests the preterite explicitly. Regional choices between simple and compound past forms remain legitimate.
learningGoals: Conjugate regular preterites.
Use frequent strong irregular stems.
Preserve sounds and common third-person changes.

rules.title: Regular -ar preterites
rules.explanation: Remove -ar and add -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. Nosotros forms can match the present; context identifies the tense.
rules.pattern: hablé; hablaste; habló; hablamos; hablasteis; hablaron
examples: Ayer compré fruta. — Yesterday I bought fruit.
El sábado descansamos. — On Saturday we rested.
commonMistakes: Keep the accents in yo -é and él/ella -ó.

rules.title: Regular -er/-ir preterites
rules.explanation: Regular -er and -ir share -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron.
rules.pattern: comí / viví; comieron / vivieron
examples: Vendí mi bicicleta. — I sold my bicycle.
Salieron temprano. — They left early.
commonMistakes: Use -ió for a regular third-person singular form, not present -e.

rules.title: Frequent irregular preterites
rules.explanation: Special stems include tuv-, estuv-, pud-, pus- and hic-. Ser and ir share fui/fuiste/fue/fuimos/fuisteis/fueron. The sentence supplies their meaning.
rules.pattern: tuve; estuvo; pudieron; pusimos; hiciste; fue
examples: Tuve una reunión. — I had a meeting.
Fue al cine. — He or she went to the cinema.
commonMistakes: These strong endings do not take the regular yo/él written accents.

rules.title: Spelling and third-person changes
rules.explanation: Yo forms in -car/-gar/-zar use -qué/-gué/-cé to preserve spelling patterns. Leer has leyó/leyeron; construir has construyó/construyeron; some -ir stem-changing verbs change e→i or o→u in third persons.
rules.pattern: busqué; llegué; empecé; leyó; pidió
examples: Busqué el recibo. — I looked for the receipt.
Pidió una sopa. — He or she ordered a soup.
commonMistakes: Do not apply a present e→ie pattern to a preterite third person such as pidió.

introduction: The preterite, also called pretérito perfecto simple or indefinido, views a past situation as a completed whole. A long event can use it when the speaker presents its full span.
Regular -ar endings differ from -er/-ir. Many strong irregular preterites use a special stem without the written accents of regular endings.

topics.title: The imperfect: past habits and background
topics.summary: Form the imperfect and present past situations without focusing on their endpoints.
topics.guidance: Past habits, descriptions and ongoing backgrounds often use the imperfect. Context and viewpoint matter; a time word alone never decides everything.
learningGoals: Conjugate -aba and -ía imperfect forms.
Use era, iba and veía.
Describe past habits, ages, time and ongoing situations.

rules.title: Regular -ar imperfect
rules.explanation: Use -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban after the stem. Yo and third-person singular share a form.
rules.pattern: hablaba; hablabas; hablábamos; hablaban
examples: Antes trabajaba de noche. — I used to work at night.
Jugábamos en el patio. — We used to play in the yard.
commonMistakes: Nosotros -ábamos needs an accent.

rules.title: Regular -er/-ir imperfect
rules.explanation: Use -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. All these endings carry an accent on í.
rules.pattern: comía; vivías; teníamos; dormían
examples: Vivíamos cerca del río. — We used to live near the river.
Tenía diez años. — I was ten years old.
commonMistakes: Do not add present stem changes: use dormía, not duermía.

rules.title: Ser, ir and ver
rules.explanation: Learn era/eras/era/éramos/erais/eran; iba/ibas/iba/íbamos/ibais/iban; veía/veías/veía/veíamos/veíais/veían.
rules.pattern: era; iba; veía
examples: Éramos vecinos. — We used to be neighbours.
Iban a pie. — They used to go on foot.
commonMistakes: Ver retains e in veía.

rules.title: Present the background
rules.explanation: Use the imperfect to set a scene, describe a habitual past, or give age/time within a past narrative. The construction focuses on a situation, not its whole completed span.
rules.pattern: era de noche; tenía ocho años; mientras leía
examples: Hacía frío cuando llegamos. — It was cold when we arrived.
Mientras cocinaba, escuchaba música. — While cooking, I was listening to music.
commonMistakes: Do not claim an imperfect situation has no possible endpoint.

introduction: The imperfect presents a past situation from within its development or as a background or habit. It does not by itself assert that the situation never ended.
Its main irregular verbs are ser, ir and ver. Present-tense stem changes do not carry over to ordinary imperfect forms.

topics.title: Preterite or imperfect: choosing a viewpoint
topics.summary: Contrast completed events, habits, background situations and changes of meaning.
topics.guidance: Read the requested viewpoint. Several sentences can be grammatical with either tense but mean something different.
learningGoals: Present events as completed wholes.
Present past habits and backgrounds.
Recognise contrasts such as knew versus found out.

rules.title: Present a completed whole
rules.explanation: Use the preterite when the intended viewpoint presents a past event or span as complete, often advancing a narrative.
rules.pattern: event as a whole → preterite
examples: Vivió allí cinco años y después se mudó. — She lived there five years and then moved.
Llegó y abrió la puerta. — He arrived and opened the door.
commonMistakes: A long duration can still be viewed as a completed whole.

rules.title: Present a past habit
rules.explanation: Use the imperfect when describing a repeated background routine without presenting its total boundaries. The preterite can instead summarise an entire series.
rules.pattern: past routine from within → imperfect
examples: De pequeña leía cada noche. — As a child I used to read every night.
Entonces íbamos en autobús. — Back then we used to go by bus.
commonMistakes: Do not claim repeated actions always require imperfect.

rules.title: Separate background and event
rules.explanation: An ongoing background often uses imperfect while a foreground event uses preterite. Two simultaneous backgrounds can both be imperfect; event sequences can both be preterite.
rules.pattern: mientras + background; cuando + event in the stated reading
examples: Mientras cocinaba, llegó el cartero. — While I was cooking, the postman arrived.
El viento soplaba y las hojas caían. — The wind was blowing and leaves were falling.
commonMistakes: Cuando itself does not force preterite.

rules.title: Notice meaning contrasts
rules.explanation: In suitable contexts, sabía expresses existing knowledge and supe finding out; conocía can express familiarity and conocí a first meeting. No quise can report refusal; podía reports capacity, while pude can report a successful achievement.
rules.pattern: sabía / supe; conocía / conocí; podía / pude
examples: Supe la noticia al abrir el mensaje. — I found out the news on opening the message.
Ya conocía a la directora. — I already knew the director.
commonMistakes: These are contextual interpretations, not rigid translations in every possible sentence.

introduction: The choice is about how the speaker presents a situation, not simply whether it lasted a long time. Vivió allí veinte años can give a completed span; vivía allí describes a background residence.
Words such as siempre, ayer and cuando do not mechanically select a tense. The tasks specify the intended reading so an alternative viewpoint is not labelled universally ungrammatical.

topics.title: Present perfect and pluperfect
topics.summary: Build compound past forms with haber and relate an earlier event to a reference time.
topics.guidance: Perfect usage varies substantially across Spanish-speaking regions. Form questions name the required tense instead of penalising another valid regional tense choice.
learningGoals: Conjugate present-perfect haber.
Form regular and common irregular participles.
Use the pluperfect for an earlier past.

rules.title: Conjugate the auxiliary
rules.explanation: Present-perfect auxiliaries are he, has, ha, hemos, habéis and han. The auxiliary agrees with the subject.
rules.pattern: he hablado; has comido; han salido
examples: He perdido mi llave. — I have lost my key.
Hemos terminado el trabajo. — We have finished the work.
commonMistakes: Use hemos rather than archaic habemos in the ordinary compound perfect.

rules.title: Form regular participles
rules.explanation: Regular -ar verbs form -ado and regular -er/-ir verbs form -ido. After haber, the participle stays unchanged for gender and number.
rules.pattern: hablar → hablado; comer → comido; vivir → vivido
examples: Ella ha viajado mucho. — She has travelled a lot.
Ellas han llegado. — They have arrived.
commonMistakes: Do not make the haber participle agree with a feminine or plural subject.

rules.title: Learn irregular participles
rules.explanation: Frequent irregular participles include abierto, dicho, hecho, escrito, visto, vuelto and puesto. Learn them with the infinitive.
rules.pattern: abrir → abierto; hacer → hecho; ver → visto
examples: He abierto la ventana. — I have opened the window.
Han escrito una carta. — They have written a letter.
commonMistakes: Do not invent regular forms such as hacido or escribido.

rules.title: Locate the earlier past
rules.explanation: Use había/habías/había/habíamos/habíais/habían plus a participle to mark completion before another past point.
rules.pattern: cuando llegó, ya había salido
examples: Cuando llamaste, ya había cenado. — When you called, I had already eaten dinner.
El tren ya había salido. — The train had already left.
commonMistakes: Had in this construction is auxiliary haber, not possession tener.

introduction: The present perfect combines present haber with a participle. It can connect a past experience or result with a present reference period, but its distribution differs greatly across regions. A simple preterite is often normal where another variety uses a compound perfect.
The pluperfect uses imperfect haber to present something completed before another past reference point. With auxiliary haber, the participle is invariable: ellas han llegado, not llegadas.

topics.title: Future and conditional forms
topics.summary: Form future and conditional verbs and use them for predictions, hypotheses and future-in-the-past.
topics.guidance: Other future expressions, such as the present or ir a + infinitive, are valid in many contexts. These form tasks explicitly request the simple future or conditional.
learningGoals: Build regular and common irregular future forms.
Form the conditional using shared endings.
Recognise polite, hypothetical and future-in-the-past uses.

rules.title: Regular simple future
rules.explanation: Keep the infinitive and add -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. The same endings serve -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
rules.pattern: hablaré; comerás; vivirá; viajaremos
examples: Mañana estudiaré en casa. — Tomorrow I will study at home.
Abrirán una tienda. — They will open a shop.
commonMistakes: Do not remove the infinitive ending as for the present.

rules.title: Irregular future stems
rules.explanation: Use special stems such as tendr-, podr-, saldr-, pondr-, dir- and har-, followed by the ordinary future endings.
rules.pattern: tendré; podrás; saldrá; diremos
examples: Tendré tiempo mañana. — I will have time tomorrow.
Haremos una pausa. — We will take a break.
commonMistakes: The irregularity is in the stem, not a new set of person endings.

rules.title: Build the conditional
rules.explanation: Add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían to the infinitive or the same irregular stem used in the future. All these endings have accented í.
rules.pattern: hablaría; comerías; tendríamos; harían
examples: Con más tiempo, viajaría. — With more time, I would travel.
Podríamos esperar. — We could wait.
commonMistakes: Do not combine a regular infinitive with a verb that requires an irregular stem.

rules.title: Interpret the conditional
rules.explanation: The conditional can describe a hypothetical action, a polite request/advice, or an event later than a past statement. The intended meaning is specified in the tasks.
rules.pattern: dijo que volvería; ¿podría…?; yo descansaría
examples: Dijo que vendría después. — She said she would come later.
¿Podría ayudarme? — Could you help me?

introduction: The simple future adds endings to the infinitive or an irregular stem. Spanish also expresses plans with ir a + infinitive: Voy a estudiar. No single future form is required for every future situation.
The conditional shares irregular stems with the future. It can present a hypothesis, soften a request or place an event later than a past reporting point.

rules.title: Regular simple future
rules.explanation: Keep the infinitive and add -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. The same endings serve -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
rules.pattern: hablaré; comerás; vivirá; viajaremos
examples: Mañana estudiaré en casa. — Tomorrow I will study at home.
Abrirán una tienda. — They will open a shop.
commonMistakes: Do not remove the infinitive ending as for the present.

rules.title: Irregular future stems
rules.explanation: Use special stems such as tendr-, podr-, saldr-, pondr-, dir- and har-, followed by the ordinary future endings.
rules.pattern: tendré; podrás; saldrá; diremos
examples: Tendré tiempo mañana. — I will have time tomorrow.
Haremos una pausa. — We will take a break.
commonMistakes: The irregularity is in the stem, not a new set of person endings.

rules.title: Build the conditional
rules.explanation: Add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían to the infinitive or the same irregular stem used in the future. All these endings have accented í.
rules.pattern: hablaría; comerías; tendríamos; harían
examples: Con más tiempo, viajaría. — With more time, I would travel.
Podríamos esperar. — We could wait.
commonMistakes: Do not combine a regular infinitive with a verb that requires an irregular stem.

rules.title: Interpret the conditional
rules.explanation: The conditional can describe a hypothetical action, a polite request/advice, or an event later than a past statement. The intended meaning is specified in the tasks.
rules.pattern: dijo que volvería; ¿podría…?; yo descansaría
examples: Dijo que vendría después. — She said she would come later.
¿Podría ayudarme? — Could you help me?
commonMistakes: A conditional request is a way to soften a request, not a claim about future certainty.

topics.title: Direct and indirect object pronouns
topics.summary: Object pronouns connect an action to what is affected and to its recipient. Identify the function before choosing gender and number.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Replace the direct object
Name the recipient
Use me, te and nos
Place a clitic before a finite verb

rules.title: Replace the direct object
rules.explanation: Lo, la, los and las replace third-person direct objects. Match the noun’s grammatical gender and number. This chapter uses inanimate objects so accepted personal leísmo does not create competing answers.
rules.pattern: Verb + thing → lo / la / los / las + finite verb
examples: La maleta pesa; la llevo yo. — The suitcase is heavy; I will carry it.
Compré los billetes y los guardé. — I bought the tickets and put them away.
commonMistakes: Do not choose le merely because the object follows a verb.

rules.title: Name the recipient
rules.explanation: Le and les represent third-person indirect objects. They distinguish singular and plural recipients, not masculine and feminine. A following a-phrase can clarify the recipient.
rules.pattern: le = to him / her / you; les = to them / you plural
examples: Le envié una foto a mi hermana. — I sent my sister a photo.
Les preparé café a los invitados. — I made the guests coffee.
commonMistakes: Do not make le feminine or make it agree with the gift.

rules.title: Use me, te and nos
rules.explanation: Me, te and nos can be direct or indirect objects. Their form follows the person referred to; the verb and context reveal their function.
rules.pattern: me = me / to me; te = you / to you; nos = us / to us
examples: ¿Me oyes? — Can you hear me?
Nos mandaron el horario. — They sent us the timetable.
commonMistakes: Do not use a third-person pronoun for the speaker.

rules.title: Place a clitic before a finite verb
rules.explanation: In ordinary contemporary statements, object clitics precede a simple finite verb. In a compound tense they precede the auxiliary haber; they do not sit between haber and its participle.
rules.pattern: clitic + conjugated verb; clitic + haber + participle
examples: La he leído dos veces. — I have read it twice.
No los conozco. — I do not know them.
commonMistakes: Do not insert a pronoun between he and leído.

topics.title: Two pronouns and their placement
topics.summary: When an action has both a recipient and an object, Spanish puts the recipient pronoun first. Placement depends on the verb form.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Change le or les to se before lo or la
Keep the recipient before the thing
Attach pronouns to infinitives and gerunds
Attach in affirmative commands; precede in negatives

rules.title: Change le or les to se before lo or la
rules.explanation: Le and les become se immediately before lo, la, los or las. Se does not show the number of recipients; the following pronoun agrees with the thing.
rules.pattern: le / les + lo / la / los / las → se + lo / la / los / las
examples: El plano: se lo di a Clara. — I gave it to Clara.
Las fotos: se las mandé a mis primos. — I sent them to my cousins.
commonMistakes: Never write le lo or les las.

rules.title: Keep the recipient before the thing
rules.explanation: Me, te and nos do not change to se. They come before the direct-object pronoun.
rules.pattern: me / te / nos + lo / la / los / las
examples: ¿Me lo explicas? — Can you explain it to me?
Te las guardo. — I will keep them for you.
commonMistakes: Do not reverse me lo to lo me.

rules.title: Attach pronouns to infinitives and gerunds
rules.explanation: With a verb phrase such as poder hacer or estar leyendo, both clitics may precede the finite verb or attach together to the infinitive or gerund. Do not split the pair. Written accents may be needed.
rules.pattern: Se lo puedo dar = Puedo dárselo; se lo estoy leyendo = estoy leyéndoselo
examples: Voy a explicártelo. — I am going to explain it to you.
Estoy mostrándoselas. — I am showing them to him/her/them.
commonMistakes: Do not put one clitic before the auxiliary and attach the other.

rules.title: Attach in affirmative commands; precede in negatives
rules.explanation: Affirmative imperatives take attached clitics. Negative commands put the clitics before the subjunctive verb. Accents preserve the original stress.
rules.pattern: Dímelo. / No me lo digas.
examples: Tráemelas. — Bring them to me.
No se lo cuentes. — Do not tell him/her/them.
commonMistakes: Do not attach clitics after a negative command.

topics.title: Por, para and other prepositions
topics.summary: Prepositions show relationships such as cause, destination, means and time. Translate the relationship in context rather than assigning one English word to each preposition.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Use por for cause, exchange and means
Use para for purpose, recipient and deadline
Show position, direction and origin
Learn time and dependent combinations

rules.title: Use por for cause, exchange and means
rules.explanation: Por can identify a cause, route, exchange, agent or means of communication. The intended relationship distinguishes it from para.
rules.pattern: por + cause / route / exchange / means
examples: Gracias por tu paciencia. — Thank you for your patience.
Lo envié por correo. — I sent it by post.
commonMistakes: Do not use para after gracias when giving the reason for thanks.

rules.title: Use para for purpose, recipient and deadline
rules.explanation: Para commonly names a purpose, intended recipient or deadline. An infinitive can state a purpose when the subject remains the same.
rules.pattern: para + infinitive / intended recipient / deadline
examples: Estudio para aprender. — I study in order to learn.
El paquete es para usted. — The parcel is for you.
commonMistakes: Do not confuse the goal of an action with its cause.

rules.title: Show position, direction and origin

topics.title: Comparison and quantity
topics.summary: Compare qualities and amounts with matching structures. Some comparison words are invariable; quantity words that accompany nouns often agree.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Build unequal comparisons
Compare equal qualities and amounts
Identify an extreme within a group
Match quantity words to nouns

rules.title: Build unequal comparisons
rules.explanation: Más or menos + adjective/adverb + que compares unequal qualities. Mejor and peor are irregular comparisons; do not normally add más to them.
rules.pattern: más / menos + adjective + que; mejor / peor que
examples: Este puente es más largo que el otro. — This bridge is longer than the other.
Hoy me siento mejor que ayer. — I feel better today than yesterday.
commonMistakes: Do not use más mejor for the ordinary comparative.

rules.title: Compare equal qualities and amounts
rules.explanation: Tan + adjective/adverb + como compares qualities. Tanto agrees with a noun in gender and number; as an adverb with a verb it stays tanto.
rules.pattern: tan alto como; tanta agua como; trabaja tanto como
examples: Es tan ancho como la puerta. — It is as wide as the door.
Tengo tantas dudas como tú. — I have as many doubts as you.
commonMistakes: Do not put tan directly before a noun when quantifying it.

rules.title: Identify an extreme within a group
rules.explanation: A relative superlative uses a definite article with más or menos and a comparison group introduced by de. Mejor, peor, mayor and menor can also occur in this structure.
rules.pattern: el / la / los / las + más / menos + adjective + de
examples: Es la calle más estrecha del barrio. — It is the narrowest street in the neighborhood.
Son los mejores asientos de la sala. — They are the best seats in the room.
commonMistakes: Use de, rather than que, to introduce the whole comparison group.

rules.title: Match quantity words to nouns
rules.explanation: Mucho, poco, demasiado and suficiente can quantify nouns. Variable forms agree with the noun; muy modifies an adjective or adverb. Muy is invariable.
rules.pattern: mucho trabajo; muchas tareas; muy difícil
examples: Hay demasiadas cajas. — There are too many boxes.
La prueba es muy difícil. — The test is very difficult.
commonMistakes: Do not say muy libros or mucho difícil.

topics.title: Infinitives, gerunds and verbal phrases
topics.summary: Infinitives and gerunds combine with finite verbs to express ability, obligation, progress and stages of an action.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Use infinitives after modal and impersonal patterns
Form gerunds, including irregulars
Describe progress and continuing activity
Mark starting, stopping, repeating and recent completion

rules.title: Use infinitives after modal and impersonal patterns
rules.explanation: Poder, querer and deber take an infinitive directly. Tener que and hay que include que. In ordinary non-epistemic obligation, deber + infinitive is a clear pattern.
rules.pattern: puedo salir; quiero aprender; tengo que trabajar; hay que esperar
examples: Podemos entrar. — We can go in.
Hay que reservar. — It is necessary to book.
commonMistakes: Do not conjugate the second verb after puedo.

rules.title: Form gerunds, including irregulars
rules.explanation: Regular -ar verbs form -ando and -er/-ir verbs form -iendo. Some forms have a stem change or y: diciendo, durmiendo, leyendo, yendo.
rules.pattern: hablar → hablando; comer → comiendo; leer → leyendo
examples: Estoy leyendo una novela. — I am reading a novel.
El bebé está durmiendo. — The baby is sleeping.
commonMistakes: Do not form leer as leiendo or ir as iendo.

rules.title: Describe progress and continuing activity
rules.explanation: Estar + gerund presents an action in progress. Seguir + gerund means to continue. Llevar + duration + gerund measures how long an activity has continued.
rules.pattern: está trabajando; sigue esperando; lleva dos horas estudiando
examples: Sigo buscando las llaves. — I am still looking for the keys.
Llevo media hora esperando. — I have been waiting for half an hour.
commonMistakes: Do not use an infinitive after seguir when it means continue doing.

rules.title: Mark starting, stopping, repeating and recent completion
rules.explanation: Empezar a marks a beginning, dejar de a stopping point, volver a a repetition and acabar de a very recent completion. Each phrase keeps its preposition before an infinitive.
rules.pattern: empezar a; dejar de; volver a; acabar de + infinitive
examples: Volvió a llamar. — He/she called again.
Acabo de llegar. — I have just arrived.
commonMistakes: Do not omit the preposition that belongs to the verbal phrase.

topics.title: Forming the present subjunctive
topics.summary: The subjunctive is a mood used in selected dependent clauses and commands. First learn its present-tense forms; the following chapters explain when those forms are needed.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Form regular -ar subjunctives
Form regular -er and -ir subjunctives
Preserve stems and spelling changes
Learn the core irregular forms

rules.title: Form regular -ar subjunctives
rules.explanation: Regular -ar verbs use -e, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en in the present subjunctive. These endings differ from the present indicative.
rules.pattern: hablar → hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen
examples: Espero que descanses. — I hope you rest.
Es mejor que caminemos. — It is better for us to walk.
commonMistakes: Do not keep the indicative -as ending in the tú subjunctive.

rules.title: Form regular -er and -ir subjunctives
rules.explanation: Regular -er and -ir verbs share -a, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an in the present subjunctive.
rules.pattern: comer → coma; vivir → viva; aprender → aprendamos
examples: Quiero que aprendas. — I want you to learn.
Ojalá reciban la carta. — I hope they receive the letter.
commonMistakes: Do not use indicative -en where the subjunctive needs -an.

rules.title: Preserve stems and spelling changes
rules.explanation: Many present subjunctives use the yo indicative stem. Spelling changes preserve sound: buscar → busque, llegar → llegue. Stem-changing -ir verbs can also change in nosotros: pedir → pidamos, dormir → durmamos.
rules.pattern: tengo → tenga; busco → busque; pido → pida / pidamos
examples: Quiero que busques otra solución. — I want you to look for another solution.
Es mejor que durmamos. — It is better for us to sleep.
commonMistakes: Nosotros forms of -ir stem-changers need special attention.

rules.title: Learn the core irregular forms
rules.explanation: Ser, ir, haber, saber, estar and dar have important irregular present subjunctives: sea, vaya, haya, sepa, esté and dé. The accents in esté and dé distinguish forms and stress.
rules.pattern: sea; vaya; haya; sepa; esté; dé
examples: Espero que sea fácil. — I hope it is easy.
Ojalá haya sitio. — I hope there is room.
commonMistakes: Existential haya stays singular even before a plural noun.

topics.title: Wishes, feelings and evaluation
topics.summary: Spanish often uses the subjunctive when one person influences another, reacts emotionally to an event or evaluates what should happen. An infinitive is common when the subject stays the same.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Express wishes and influence
React to events
Evaluate what should happen
Use an infinitive for a shared subject or general action

rules.title: Express wishes and influence
rules.explanation: Querer que, pedir que and recomendar que introduce subjunctive clauses when they concern another subject. The main verb expresses a wish or influence rather than reporting a fact.
rules.pattern: quiero / pido / recomiendo + que + subjunctive
examples: Quiero que vengas. — I want you to come.
Recomiendo que reserve. — I recommend that he/she book.
commonMistakes: Do not copy English want someone to as querer alguien a.

rules.title: React to events
rules.explanation: Alegrarse de que, sentir que in its regret sense and dar pena que can introduce subjunctive clauses. Emotional evaluation does not mean the event is untrue: a known fact can still be in the subjunctive.
rules.pattern: me alegra / me da pena / siento + que + subjunctive
examples: Me alegra que estés aquí. — I am glad you are here.
Siento que no puedas venir. — I am sorry you cannot come.
commonMistakes: Subjunctive is not simply a synonym for unreal.

rules.title: Evaluate what should happen
rules.explanation: Es necesario que, es importante que and es mejor que normally take the subjunctive. They differ from factual assertions such as es cierto que.
rules.pattern: es necesario / importante / mejor + que + subjunctive
examples: Es necesario que firmes. — You need to sign.
Es mejor que esperemos. — It is better for us to wait.
commonMistakes: Do not assume every es…que phrase takes the same mood.

rules.title: Use an infinitive for a shared subject or general action
rules.explanation: When the same person wants and acts, querer + infinitive is the normal compact pattern. A general evaluation without a named subject can also take an infinitive: es importante descansar.
rules.pattern: quiero + infinitive; me alegro de + infinitive; es importante + infinitive
examples: Quiero descansar. — I want to rest.
Es importante beber agua. — Drinking water is important.
commonMistakes: Do not put a conjugated verb directly after quiero without que.

introduction: Spanish often uses the subjunctive when one person influences another, reacts emotionally to an event or evaluates what should happen. An infinitive is common when the subject stays the same.

rules.title: Express wishes and influence
rules.explanation: Querer que, pedir que and recomendar que introduce subjunctive clauses when they concern another subject. The main verb expresses a wish or influence rather than reporting a fact.
rules.pattern: quiero / pido / recomiendo + que + subjunctive
examples: Quiero que vengas. — I want you to come.
Recomiendo que reserve. — I recommend that he/she book.
commonMistakes: Do not copy English want someone to as querer alguien a.

rules.title: React to events
rules.explanation: Alegrarse de que, sentir que in its regret sense and dar pena que can introduce subjunctive clauses. Emotional evaluation does not mean the event is untrue: a known fact can still be in the subjunctive.
rules.pattern: me alegra / me da pena / siento + que + subjunctive
examples: Me alegra que estés aquí. — I am glad you are here.
Siento que no puedas venir. — I am sorry you cannot come.
commonMistakes: Subjunctive is not simply a synonym for unreal.

rules.title: Evaluate what should happen
rules.explanation: Es necesario que, es importante que and es mejor que normally take the subjunctive. They differ from factual assertions such as es cierto que.
rules.pattern: es necesario / importante / mejor + que + subjunctive
examples: Es necesario que firmes. — You need to sign.
Es mejor que esperemos. — It is better for us to wait.
commonMistakes: Do not assume every es…que phrase takes the same mood.

rules.title: Use an infinitive for a shared subject or general action
rules.explanation: When the same person wants and acts, querer + infinitive is the normal compact pattern. A general evaluation without a named subject can also take an infinitive: es importante descansar.
rules.pattern: quiero + infinitive; me alegro de + infinitive; es importante + infinitive
examples: Quiero descansar. — I want to rest.
Es importante beber agua. — Drinking water is important.
commonMistakes: Do not put a conjugated verb directly after quiero without que.

topics.title: Doubt, purpose and unknown referents
topics.summary: Mood signals how a speaker presents information. Doubt, a purpose that is to be achieved and a sought or nonexistent referent often call for the subjunctive.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Use the subjunctive in doubt and denial
Express purpose with para que
Describe a sought or nonexistent referent
Use the indicative for asserted facts

rules.title: Use the subjunctive in doubt and denial
rules.explanation: Dudar que and no creer que commonly introduce the subjunctive when the speaker withholds belief. Affirmative creer que ordinarily reports a belief with the indicative.
rules.pattern: dudo que / no creo que + subjunctive
examples: Dudo que sea suficiente. — I doubt it is enough.
No creo que tengan la llave. — I do not think they have the key.
commonMistakes: A negative main verb does not automatically select subjunctive in every construction; learn the pattern and meaning.

rules.title: Express purpose with para que
rules.explanation: Para que introduces an intended outcome, normally with a different subject, and takes the subjunctive. Para + infinitive commonly expresses a goal with the same subject.
rules.pattern: para + infinitive; para que + subjunctive
examples: Te lo explico para que lo entiendas. — I explain it so you understand.
Salgo pronto para evitar el tráfico. — I leave early to avoid traffic.
commonMistakes: Do not put an indicative verb after para que for an intended outcome.

rules.title: Describe a sought or nonexistent referent
rules.explanation: A relative clause often takes the subjunctive when the speaker seeks a person or thing without asserting that a matching one exists. A known, identified referent normally takes the indicative.
rules.pattern: busco / necesito + an unidentified noun + que + subjunctive
examples: Busco un piso que tenga ascensor. — I seek a flat with a lift.
No hay nadie que conozca la clave. — Nobody knows the code.
commonMistakes: Busco does not force subjunctive if the person sought is already identified; the speaker’s meaning matters.

rules.title: Use the indicative for asserted facts
rules.explanation: Affirmative statements of belief, knowledge and certainty commonly use indicative clauses. A relative describing an identified person or thing also commonly uses the indicative.
rules.pattern: sé / creo / es cierto + que + indicative; known noun + que + indicative
examples: Sé que vive aquí. — I know he/she lives here.
Tengo un piso que tiene ascensor. — I have a flat with a lift.
commonMistakes: Do not use subjunctive just because a clause starts with que.

topics.title: Giving instructions and commands
topics.summary: Command forms depend on the person addressed and on whether the instruction is positive or negative. This chapter names tú, usted, ustedes or vosotros so regional address choices are clear.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Give affirmative tú commands
Give negative tú commands
Address usted and ustedes
Use vosotros commands and shared suggestions

rules.title: Give affirmative tú commands
rules.explanation: Regular affirmative tú commands usually match the third-person singular present indicative. Key irregulars include di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten and ven.
rules.pattern: habla; come; abre; di; haz; ven
examples: Abre la puerta. — Open the door.
Ven conmigo. — Come with me.
commonMistakes: Do not use the infinitive as the ordinary written tú command.

rules.title: Give negative tú commands
rules.explanation: Negative tú commands use no + present subjunctive. Their forms differ from affirmative tú commands, especially with irregular verbs.
rules.pattern: no hables; no comas; no abras; no vayas
examples: No corras. — Do not run.
No hagas ruido. — Do not make noise.
commonMistakes: Do not put no in front of an affirmative tú imperative.

rules.title: Address usted and ustedes
rules.explanation: Usted and ustedes commands use present subjunctive forms in both positive and negative instructions. Usted takes singular forms; ustedes takes plural forms.
rules.pattern: usted: pase / no pase; ustedes: pasen / no pasen
examples: Firme aquí, por favor. — Please sign here.
No entren todavía. — Do not come in yet.
commonMistakes: Do not confuse respectful singular usted with plural ustedes.

rules.title: Use vosotros commands and shared suggestions
rules.explanation: Affirmative vosotros commands usually replace infinitive -r with -d. Negative vosotros uses the subjunctive. Nosotros suggestions also use the subjunctive; with reflexive nos, the final -s drops before attachment.
rules.pattern: hablad / no habléis; salgamos; sentémonos
examples: Leed el aviso. — Read the notice (vosotros).
Sentémonos aquí. — Let us sit here.
commonMistakes: These vosotros forms are used in much of Spain; ustedes is normal for plural address in most of the Americas.

topics.title: Time, conditions and concession
topics.summary: Time and concessive clauses can use different moods according to whether an event is asserted, habitual, expected or left open. The context, not a single trigger word, determines the meaning.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Use subjunctive for pending time events
Use indicative for asserted habits and past events
Distinguish asserted and open concessions
Use provided-that and unless clauses

rules.title: Use subjunctive for pending time events
rules.explanation: Cuando, en cuanto and hasta que normally take the subjunctive when the event is still pending. Spanish does not ordinarily use a future indicative after cuando in this time-clause pattern.
rules.pattern: cuando / en cuanto / hasta que + subjunctive for a pending event
examples: Te llamaré cuando llegue. — I will call when I arrive.
Esperaremos hasta que abran. — We will wait until they open.
commonMistakes: Do not transfer English future will into the pending cuando-clause.

rules.title: Use indicative for asserted habits and past events
rules.explanation: Cuando and mientras can take the indicative for events asserted as real or repeated. A habitual present differs from a pending single future event.
rules.pattern: cuando + indicative for an asserted habit or completed event
examples: Cuando llueve, llevo botas. — When it rains, I wear boots.
Cuando llegué, la tienda estaba cerrada. — When I arrived, the shop was closed.
commonMistakes: Cuando is not an automatic subjunctive trigger.

rules.title: Distinguish asserted and open concessions
rules.explanation: Aunque with the indicative commonly presents the obstacle as asserted. With the subjunctive it can present an unknown possibility or background an obstacle as irrelevant. Both moods can be valid with different meanings, so exercises specify the intended reading.
rules.pattern: aunque + indicative = asserted obstacle; aunque + subjunctive = open or backgrounded obstacle
examples: Aunque está lejos, voy. — Although it is far, I am going.
Aunque esté lejos, iré. — Even if it is far, I will go.
commonMistakes: Do not label either mood universally wrong after aunque.

rules.title: Use provided-that and unless clauses
rules.explanation: Con tal de que, a menos que and a condición de que introduce conditional circumstances with the subjunctive. Ordinary open si-conditions use the indicative instead.
rules.pattern: con tal de que / a menos que + subjunctive; si + present indicative
examples: Iré con tal de que vengas. — I will go provided you come.
Salimos si no llueve. — We go out if it does not rain.
commonMistakes: Do not generalize the subjunctive of a menos que to an ordinary present si-clause.

topics.title: Past subjunctives and hypothetical conditions
topics.summary: Past subjunctive forms appear after past wishes and in hypothetical conditions. They can refer to present unreality as well as past time; the whole construction determines the time reference.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Form the imperfect subjunctive
Place a regretted event before a past reference point
Build hypothetical present or future conditions
Build unreal past conditions and results

rules.title: Form the imperfect subjunctive
rules.explanation: The imperfect subjunctive is built from the third-person plural preterite without -ron, then -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran. The parallel -se forms are also valid. Nosotros forms carry a written accent before -ramos.
rules.pattern: hablaron → hablara; tuvieron → tuviera; fuéramos
examples: Quería que vinieras. — I wanted you to come.
Nos pidieron que habláramos. — They asked us to speak.
commonMistakes: The -ra and -se series are both standard; this practice asks for -ra forms without rejecting -se.

rules.title: Place a regretted event before a past reference point
rules.explanation: The pluperfect subjunctive combines hubiera or hubiese with a past participle. It can express an earlier event after a past emotional reaction or an unreal past wish.
rules.pattern: hubiera / hubiese + past participle
examples: Sentí que no hubieras venido. — I was sorry you had not come.
Ojalá hubiéramos reservado. — If only we had booked.
commonMistakes: Do not use conditional habría where a past reaction selects subjunctive.

rules.title: Build hypothetical present or future conditions
rules.explanation: A remote or contrary-to-fact condition commonly uses si + imperfect subjunctive and a conditional result. Ordinary open conditions use a different pattern, si + present indicative.
rules.pattern: si + imperfect subjunctive, conditional
examples: Si tuviera tiempo, iría. — If I had time, I would go.
Si viviéramos cerca, nos veríamos más. — If we lived nearby, we would see one another more.
commonMistakes: Do not use conditional tendría in this si-clause.

rules.title: Build unreal past conditions and results
rules.explanation: An unreal past condition uses si + pluperfect subjunctive. A conditional perfect can express the unreal result. A pluperfect subjunctive can also be valid in many result clauses, so it is not treated as a wrong alternative.
rules.pattern: si + hubiera / hubiese + participle, habría + participle
examples: Si hubieras avisado, habría ido. — If you had told me, I would have gone.
Si hubiéramos salido antes, habríamos llegado. — If we had left earlier, we would have arrived.
commonMistakes: In the condition clause, do not replace hubiera with habría.

rules.title: Place a regretted event before a past reference point
rules.explanation: The pluperfect subjunctive combines hubiera or hubiese with a past participle. It can express an earlier event after a past emotional reaction or an unreal past wish.
rules.pattern: hubiera / hubiese + past participle
examples: Sentí que no hubieras venido. — I was sorry you had not come.
Ojalá hubiéramos reservado. — If only we had booked.
commonMistakes: Do not use conditional habría where a past reaction selects subjunctive.

rules.title: Build hypothetical present or future conditions
rules.explanation: A remote or contrary-to-fact condition commonly uses si + imperfect subjunctive and a conditional result. Ordinary open conditions use a different pattern, si + present indicative.
rules.pattern: si + imperfect subjunctive, conditional
examples: Si tuviera tiempo, iría. — If I had time, I would go.
Si viviéramos cerca, nos veríamos más. — If we lived nearby, we would see one another more.
commonMistakes: Do not use conditional tendría in this si-clause.

rules.title: Build unreal past conditions and results
rules.explanation: An unreal past condition uses si + pluperfect subjunctive. A conditional perfect can express the unreal result. A pluperfect subjunctive can also be valid in many result clauses, so it is not treated as a wrong alternative.
rules.pattern: si + hubiera / hubiese + participle, habría + participle
examples: Si hubieras avisado, habría ido. — If you had told me, I would have gone.
Si hubiéramos salido antes, habríamos llegado. — If we had left earlier, we would have arrived.
commonMistakes: In the condition clause, do not replace hubiera with habría.

recap: The imperfect subjunctive is built from the third-person plural preterite without -ron, then -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran. The parallel -se forms are also valid. Nosotros forms carry a written accent before -ramos.

topics.title: Relative clauses and pronouns
topics.summary: Relative clauses describe nouns or refer to an idea. Choose forms according to their role, required preposition and whether the reference is a person, possession, place or whole proposition.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Link descriptions with que
Keep prepositions in relative constructions
Make cuyo agree with the possession
Refer to places and whole ideas

rules.title: Link descriptions with que
rules.explanation: Unaccented que is the most general relative. It can refer to people or things. Spanish does not omit this relative in the ordinary defining clauses practised here, even when it represents an object.
rules.pattern: noun + que + clause
examples: La persona que llamó dejó su número. — The person who called left a number.
El libro que compré es nuevo. — The book I bought is new.
commonMistakes: Do not confuse relative que with interrogative qué.

rules.title: Keep prepositions in relative constructions
rules.explanation: A relative retains the preposition required by its role: la persona con quien trabajo, el tema del que hablamos. Quien/quienes refers to people; el que and el cual series can refer to people or things with appropriate agreement.
rules.pattern: con quien; de la que; por el que; a quienes
examples: La mujer con quien hablé es la directora. — The woman I spoke with is the director.
Ese es el asunto del que hablamos. — That is the matter we discussed.
commonMistakes: Do not leave a required preposition stranded at the end as in English.

rules.title: Make cuyo agree with the possession
rules.explanation: Cuyo, cuya, cuyos and cuyas mean whose. They agree with the possessed noun that follows, not with the possessor. No article is inserted between cuyo and that noun.
rules.pattern: possessor + cuyo/a/os/as + possessed noun
examples: La autora cuya novela leí viene hoy. — The author whose novel I read is coming today.
El edificio cuyos ascensores fallan está cerrado. — The building whose lifts fail is closed.
commonMistakes: Do not write cuyo la novela; whose is not cuyó.

rules.title: Refer to places and whole ideas
rules.explanation: Donde can introduce a location relative. Lo que can mean what/the thing that without a named noun; lo cual can refer back to a whole preceding proposition. Both lo que and lo cual can sometimes refer to a proposition, so examples avoid treating their overlap as an error.
rules.pattern: el lugar donde; lo que + clause; proposition, lo cual + clause
examples: Este es el pueblo donde nací. — This is the village where I was born.
No entiendo lo que dices. — I do not understand what you say.
commonMistakes: Do not put a written accent on relative donde or que.

topics.title: Passive voice and the uses of se
topics.summary: Spanish can shift attention away from an agent using a ser passive, a passive with se or an impersonal se construction. Reflexive and reciprocal se have different roles.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Build ser + participle passives
Make passive se agree with its subject
Keep impersonal se in the singular
Distinguish reflexive, reciprocal and pronominal uses

rules.title: Build ser + participle passives
rules.explanation: The ser passive makes the affected entity the grammatical subject. The participle agrees with that subject in gender and number. Por can identify the agent. Estar + participle commonly describes a resulting state instead.
rules.pattern: subject + ser + agreeing participle + por + agent
examples: La carta fue enviada ayer. — The letter was sent yesterday.
Los cuadros fueron restaurados. — The paintings were restored.
commonMistakes: After ser, the passive participle agrees; after auxiliary haber it does not.

rules.title: Make passive se agree with its subject
rules.explanation: In a passive se construction, the affected noun functions as subject. The verb agrees with it. These examples use things, avoiding the special patterns of personal objects.
rules.pattern: se + singular verb + singular subject; se + plural verb + plural subject
examples: Se vende una bicicleta. — A bicycle is for sale.
Se venden bicicletas. — Bicycles are for sale.
commonMistakes: Do not ignore the plural subject in the standard passive se pattern.

rules.title: Keep impersonal se in the singular
rules.explanation: Impersonal se has no grammatical subject and uses third-person singular. A personal direct object introduced by a does not control agreement. Intransitive and prepositional-complement examples are also singular.
rules.pattern: se + third-person singular; se entrevista a los candidatos
examples: Se vive bien aquí. — People live well here.
Se entrevistó a las candidatas. — The candidates were interviewed.
commonMistakes: Do not make the verb agree with an a-marked personal object.

rules.title: Distinguish reflexive, reciprocal and pronominal uses
rules.explanation: Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject. A plural reflexive may be reciprocal when context means each other. Some verbs are obligatorily pronominal in a meaning, such as arrepentirse; not every se expresses a passive.
rules.pattern: ella se lava; ellos se saludan; se arrepiente de
examples: Ella se peina. — She combs her own hair.
Los vecinos se ayudan mutuamente. — The neighbors help each other.
commonMistakes: Use context to distinguish themselves from each other.
