topics.title: Reporting statements, questions and requests
topics.summary: Reported language changes person, time reference and sometimes tense to fit the new viewpoint. Tense shifts are not mechanically mandatory: the exercises specify a past reporting viewpoint when a shift is requested.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Maintain a stated past reporting viewpoint
Report questions with si and accented question words
Report instructions with the subjunctive
Adjust person and reference to the reporting moment

rules.title: Maintain a stated past reporting viewpoint
rules.explanation: A past reporting viewpoint can shift a simultaneous present to imperfect, an earlier past to pluperfect and a later future to conditional. A fact still presented as current may retain a present tense, so the intended viewpoint must be explicit.
rules.pattern: dijo que estaba; explicó que había salido; anunció que vendría
examples: Dijo: «Estoy cansada». → Dijo que estaba cansada.
Anunció: «Volveré». → Anunció que volvería.
commonMistakes: Do not treat every retained present as ungrammatical; it may express continuing relevance.

rules.title: Report questions with si and accented question words
rules.explanation: A reported yes/no question uses si. Wh-questions retain the required interrogative word and its accent, such as dónde, cuándo or qué. The report normally has no question marks unless the whole sentence is itself a question.
rules.pattern: preguntó si; preguntó dónde / cuándo / qué
examples: Preguntó si teníamos reserva. — He/she asked whether we had a booking.
Quiso saber dónde estaba la estación. — He/she wanted to know where the station was.
commonMistakes: Interrogative words keep their accent in indirect questions.

rules.title: Report instructions with the subjunctive
rules.explanation: Pedir que and decir que in a directive sense introduce the subjunctive. With a past reporting verb, an imperfect subjunctive commonly expresses the requested action.
rules.pattern: me pidió que + imperfect subjunctive; me dijo que no + imperfect subjunctive
examples: Me pidió que esperara. — He/she asked me to wait.
Nos dijo que no saliéramos. — He/she told us not to leave.
commonMistakes: A reported command differs from a factual statement after dijo que.

rules.title: Adjust person and reference to the reporting moment
rules.explanation: Pronouns and expressions of time or place must fit the new speaker and moment. Mañana can become al día siguiente in a later report; aquí may become allí when the report is made elsewhere. These changes depend on the situation.
rules.pattern: original yo → reported él / ella; mañana → al día siguiente in a later narrative
examples: Dijo: «Mi coche está aquí». → Dijo que su coche estaba allí (reporting elsewhere).
El lunes dijo: «Voy mañana». → Dijo que iba al día siguiente.
commonMistakes: Time and place words do not change mechanically if the reporting situation stays the same.

topics.title: Cohesion, register and regional choices
topics.summary: Connected Spanish needs clear relationships between ideas and a consistent address system. Regional standards can differ without one being inherently wrong.
topics.guidance: Read the patterns, compare the examples, then use the stated context to choose one answer. Regional alternatives are identified where relevant.
learningGoals: Distinguish because, why and the reason
Mark contrast, correction and consequence
Keep references clear and grammatical
Keep address and regional choices consistent

rules.title: Distinguish because, why and the reason
rules.explanation: Porque introduces a cause. Por qué introduces a direct or indirect question about a reason. El porqué is a noun meaning the reason and can form a plural, los porqués.
rules.pattern: porque = because; por qué = why; el porqué = the reason
examples: No fui porque estaba enferma. — I did not go because I was ill.
No sé por qué cerraron. — I do not know why they closed.
commonMistakes: Do not remove the accent from an indirect por qué question.

rules.title: Mark contrast, correction and consequence
rules.explanation: Pero introduces contrast. Sino corrects a negated alternative and normally needs que before a finite clause. Por eso gives a consequence. A pesar de can precede a noun or infinitive; a pesar de que introduces a finite clause.
rules.pattern: no X, sino Y; no hizo X, sino que hizo Y; por eso + result
examples: No es azul, sino verde. — It is not blue but green.
Estaba cerrado; por eso volvimos. — It was closed, so we went back.
commonMistakes: Do not use sino to introduce an open if not condition.

rules.title: Keep references clear and grammatical
rules.explanation: Reference words and agreement help readers follow a text. Ellipsis can avoid repetition when the omitted material is recoverable. Neuter lo can represent an adjective or an entire idea rather than a masculine noun.
rules.pattern: una…otra; uno…otro; lo está; lo entiendo; también / tampoco
examples: ¿Está lista? Sí, lo está. — Is she ready? Yes, she is.
Yo no fui; ella tampoco. — I did not go; she did not either.
commonMistakes: Lo representing an attribute stays neuter even with a feminine subject.

rules.title: Keep address and regional choices consistent
rules.explanation: Ustedes uses third-person plural verbs. Vosotros takes second-person plural forms and is usual for familiar plural address in much of Spain. Voseo is standard in many regions; its forms vary. A course must specify the target system instead of rejecting another standard variety.
rules.pattern: ustedes hablan; vosotros habláis; vos hablás in Rioplatense present indicative
examples: Ustedes tienen la llave. — You have the key (plural).
Vos hablás muy claro. — You speak very clearly (Rioplatense voseo).
commonMistakes: Regional frequency does not make another standard form ungrammatical.

introduction: Connected Spanish needs clear relationships between ideas and a consistent address system. Regional standards can differ without one being inherently wrong.
The examples and exercises are original teaching material. These course levels describe a learning sequence, not a certified assessment.

rules.title: Distinguish because, why and the reason
rules.explanation: Porque introduces a cause. Por qué introduces a direct or indirect question about a reason. El porqué is a noun meaning the reason and can form a plural, los porqués.
rules.pattern: porque = because; por qué = why; el porqué = the reason
examples: No fui porque estaba enferma. — I did not go because I was ill.
No sé por qué cerraron. — I do not know why they closed.
commonMistakes: Do not remove the accent from an indirect por qué question.

rules.title: Mark contrast, correction and consequence
rules.explanation: Pero introduces contrast. Sino corrects a negated alternative and normally needs que before a finite clause. Por eso gives a consequence. A pesar de can precede a noun or infinitive; a pesar de que introduces a finite clause.
rules.pattern: no X, sino Y; no hizo X, sino que hizo Y; por eso + result
examples: No es azul, sino verde. — It is not blue but green.
Estaba cerrado; por eso volvimos. — It was closed, so we went back.
commonMistakes: Do not use sino to introduce an open if not condition.

rules.title: Keep references clear and grammatical
rules.explanation: Reference words and agreement help readers follow a text. Ellipsis can avoid repetition when the omitted material is recoverable. Neuter lo can represent an adjective or an entire idea rather than a masculine noun.
rules.pattern: una…otra; uno…otro; lo está; lo entiendo; también / tampoco
examples: ¿Está lista? Sí, lo está. — Is she ready? Yes, she is.
Yo no fui; ella tampoco. — I did not go; she did not either.
commonMistakes: Lo representing an attribute stays neuter even with a feminine subject.

rules.title: Keep address and regional choices consistent
rules.explanation: Ustedes uses third-person plural verbs. Vosotros takes second-person plural forms and is usual for familiar plural address in much of Spain. Voseo is standard in many regions; its forms vary. A course must specify the target system instead of rejecting another standard variety.
rules.pattern: ustedes hablan; vosotros habláis; vos hablás in Rioplatense present indicative
examples: Ustedes tienen la llave. — You have the key (plural).
Vos hablás muy claro. — You speak very clearly (Rioplatense voseo).
commonMistakes: Regional frequency does not make another standard form ungrammatical.
